section_1.title: Prerequisites & Linear Combinations
section_1.content: Define vectors as arrows in space (origin to point). Explain Linear Combination as 'scaling and adding' vectors: c1v1 + c2v2. Visualization: Use a coordinate grid to show how vectors reach different points.
section_1.example: A robot arm has two joints. Joint 1 moves vector A, Joint 2 moves vector B. The robot's hand reaches any point that is a combination of these movements.

section_2.title: The Concept of Span
section_2.content: Define Span as the set of all possible points reachable via linear combinations. Visualize this as the 'footprint' of vectors: a line (1 vector), a plane (2 non-collinear vectors), or 3D space (3 non-coplanar vectors).
section_2.example: If two vectors point in the same direction, they only span a line. If they point in different directions, they 'sweep out' a flat 2D carpet (plane).

section_3.title: Linear Dependence vs. Independence
section_3.content: Explain Linear Dependence as 'redundancy.' If one vector can be formed by others, it is redundant. If no vector can be formed by the others, they are independent. Visual cue: 'Collapsing' dimensions when vectors are redundant.
section_3.example: Three hikers walking in a line: If Hiker C follows Hiker B, Hiker C is redundant (linearly dependent). If Hiker C moves in a new direction, they add a new dimension of freedom.

section_4.title: Bases: The Minimum Building Blocks
section_4.content: Define a Basis as the minimal set of vectors that span the entire space. It must be linearly independent and span the space. This is the 'DNA' of the vector space.
section_4.example: Using standard basis vectors i=(1,0) and j=(0,1) as the 'grid' map that allows you to define any coordinate in a city grid.

section_5.title: Summary & Application
section_5.content: Synthesize: Span is the 'reach,' Dependence is the 'efficiency,' and Basis is the 'minimal coordinate system.' Connect this to data science where bases represent dimensions of features.
section_5.example: In 3D video games, the basis vectors define the world's axis; without them, the game engine wouldn't know how to place objects in space.
